question: Can simple single-atom input perturbations reveal whether a large GemNet-OC model trained on OC20 has learned chemically reasonable relationships among adsorbates, catalyst slabs, elemental identity, predicted energy, and predicted force?

key_findings.claim: Deleting an adsorbate atom changes GemNet-OC's predicted energy more than deleting a surface atom, which in turn changes it more than deleting a subsurface atom, across the sampled relaxed OC20 systems.
key_findings.evidence: For atom-by-atom deletion over 10,000 validation systems, the absolute predicted-energy change has mean/median 0.890/0.721 for adsorbates, 0.253/0.125 for surface atoms, and 0.122/0.036 for subsurface atoms; all three distributions are right-skewed. The rendered 3D examples also visually concentrate larger changes near adsorbates and the top slab layer.

anchors.section: Perturbations on adsorbate and slab atoms

key_findings.claim: Changing an atomic number to a nearby periodic-table entry often produces a smaller predicted-energy change than changing it to a more distant entry, and same-period replacements are often less disruptive than same-group replacements.
key_findings.evidence: The authors define one- and two-hop substitutions as horizontal or vertical moves on the periodic table and plot per-system mean energy changes for carbon, oxygen, and additional frequent elements. Several distributions and the single-system bar plots have the stated ordering, but appendix Figures 9-11 also show heavy concentration near zero, broad skew, and explicit elements for which the row/column ordering reverses. No formal effect size, uncertainty interval, or hypothesis test is reported.

anchors.section: Perturbations on the element of a specific atom

key_findings.claim: The positive force-versus-energy-change correlation is a useful diagnostic of agreement between GemNet-OC's separately predicted energy and force heads, but it is much weaker evidence of learned chemistry than the paper suggests.
key_findings.evidence: For every adsorbate or surface atom and coordinate, the paper displaces the atom by 0.1 angstrom opposite the sign of the predicted force component, then correlates the component magnitude with the energy increase within each system. Under the conventional relation F = -grad E, a first-order expansion already predicts delta-E approximately equals |F_k| times 0.1 for exactly this sign-selected perturbation. The mostly positive histogram therefore tests local cross-head consistency, but Pearson sign alone does not establish correct DFT forces, conservative dynamics, or a chemically meaningful internal mechanism.

anchors.section: How energy changes relate to forces

key_findings.claim: The experiments demonstrate structured model sensitivity, not faithful explanation or correctness on the perturbed configurations.
key_findings.evidence: All perturbation outcomes are predictions from the same GemNet-OC checkpoint. Atom deletion and element replacement frequently make off-distribution or physically ill-posed systems, yet the paper computes no DFT target for any perturbed state and uses no random, untrained, atomic-reference, simpler-GNN, or alternative-checkpoint control. The authors explicitly defer DFT evaluation, error-stratified analyses, and model comparisons to future work.

key_findings.claim: The paper provides an accessible OC20 debugging workflow and interactive per-system visualizations, but the analysis does not identify what representations or causal computations the network uses.
key_findings.evidence: The method changes one input atom at a time and maps the resulting scalar energy difference onto rotatable Plotly atom clouds with hover metadata. It never examines message-passing features, tests whether an attributed atom is necessary and sufficient under in-distribution interventions, compares attribution methods, or validates explanations against ground-truth motifs. Output sensitivity is called insight into what the model learned, although many different internal mechanisms can yield the same sensitivity curves.

anchors.section: Perturbations on adsorbate and slab atoms

method.core_idea: Run GemNet-OC repeatedly after controlled one-atom deletions, atomic-number substitutions, or coordinate displacements, and summarize how its energy and force outputs change at both system and dataset scale.
method.mechanism: A random sample of 10,000 final trajectory frames from OC20 validation supplies nominally relaxed catalyst-adsorbate systems. Each atom is removed to compare sensitivity across adsorbate, surface, and subsurface categories. Atomic numbers are replaced by one- or two-cell horizontal/vertical periodic-table neighbors to probe elemental similarity. Finally, adsorbate and surface atoms are shifted independently by 0.1 angstrom along each coordinate opposite the predicted force component, and within-system Pearson correlations relate absolute force components to predicted-energy changes. Plotly atom clouds and density, bar, scatter, and histogram plots expose examples and aggregate trends.
assumptions: Output change under a single input perturbation is a meaningful proxy for the importance of that atom or attribute to the model's reasoning.

Deletion of one atom, substitution of its element while fixing all coordinates, and a 0.1-angstrom coordinate shift remain sufficiently close to the OC20 training distribution for the response to be interpretable.

Differences among adsorbate, surface, and subsurface perturbations primarily reflect learned chemical interaction importance rather than composition, atom-reference energy conventions, local coordination, species frequency, or label availability.
Grid distance on the two-dimensional periodic table is an adequate scalar proxy for chemical similarity across the 56 OC20 elements.
Aggregating heterogeneous adsorbates and bulk materials without matched controls preserves a general chemical signal rather than mixture-specific confounding.
The final trajectory frame is relaxed enough that local coordinate perturbations can be interpreted with a first-order energy-force relationship.
A positive within-system Pearson correlation after choosing displacement direction from the predicted force is nontrivial evidence that separately trained heads learned a physical relationship.
One GemNet-OC checkpoint and one random validation sample are representative of model family, seed, training run, and OC20 distribution shifts.

techniques.role: Selects 10,000 nominally relaxed validation systems spanning 75 adsorbates, 4,202 bulk materials, and all 56 OC20 elements.
Measures the change in predicted system energy after removing each adsorbate, surface, or subsurface atom.
Changes atomic number to one- or two-hop same-row or same-column elements while keeping the geometry fixed.
Moves one atom by 0.1 angstrom per coordinate opposite the predicted force sign to produce an energy increase.
Computes Pearson correlation over 3N force-component magnitudes and energy changes for each system.
Colors rotatable three-dimensional atomic configurations by deletion-induced energy change and exposes atom metadata on hover.
Summarizes deletion, substitution, and correlation distributions over the validation sample.

evaluations.setting: A GemNet-OC S2EF checkpoint evaluated on the OC20 test set
evaluations.result: The analyzed model is reported to obtain 0.2411 eV energy MAE and 0.01901 eV/angstrom force MAE.
evaluations.baseline: No checkpoint, seed, or competing-model result is included in the perturbation study; the paper cites the broader OC20 leaderboard.

evaluations.setting: Atom-by-atom deletion in the final frames of 10,000 randomly sampled OC20 validation systems
evaluations.metric: Mean, standard deviation, median, and density of absolute predicted-energy change by atom category
evaluations.result: Mean/standard-deviation/median are 0.122/0.340/0.036 for subsurface, 0.253/0.459/0.125 for surface, and 0.890/0.734/0.721 for adsorbate atoms, preserving the claimed category ordering.
evaluations.baseline: The three structural categories are compared directly, without matched species/coordination controls, DFT perturbation labels, confidence intervals, or a null model.

evaluations.setting: Atomic-number substitution to one- and two-hop same-period or same-group neighbors over the same validation sample
evaluations.metric: Distribution of per-system mean predicted-energy change for each original element and substitution class
evaluations.result: Nearby and same-row substitutions often cluster closer to zero than farther or same-column substitutions; appendix plots document exceptions and strong element dependence.
evaluations.baseline: One-hop versus two-hop and row versus column categories only; no property-distance baseline, elemental reference correction, formal significance test, or DFT calculation.

evaluations.setting: Independent 0.1-angstrom coordinate perturbations for every adsorbate and surface atom in each of 10,000 systems
evaluations.metric: Per-system Pearson correlation between absolute predicted force components and predicted-energy changes; one displayed system has R = 0.678
evaluations.result: The histogram is concentrated on positive correlations, with most systems visually between roughly 0.2 and 0.9 and a peak near 0.6.
evaluations.baseline: No finite-difference gradient error, two-sided displacement, step-size sweep, DFT-force comparison, curl/path-integral test, conservative model, or shuffled-force control.

limitations: No DFT energy or force is computed for any perturbed configuration, so the analysis cannot distinguish chemically correct sensitivity from confidently structured extrapolation by the model.
Deleting an atom changes atom count, composition, charge/electron count, local graph topology, and possibly the energy reference; it is not a small or necessarily physical intervention.

Element substitution at fixed geometry can create implausible bond lengths and oxidation environments, and raw energy changes are not corrected by elemental chemical potentials or isolated-atom references.
Periodic-table Manhattan hops conflate period, group, valence, radius, electronegativity, and abundance and do not define a uniform chemical distance.

Adsorbate, surface, and subsurface categories differ systematically in element identities, coordination, counts, geometric constraints, and whether force labels are trained, leaving the category comparison confounded.

Atoms and systems are nested within repeated adsorbates and bulk materials, but the analysis reports no hierarchical bootstrap, confidence interval, hypothesis test, or control for highly imbalanced element frequencies.
The force section alternately says force is the gradient and that atoms move toward their forces, while the actual protocol moves opposite the force; the conventional relation is F = -grad E.

The sign-conditioned displacement makes positive correlation expected to first order, so it is not a stringent test of physical consistency; Pearson correlation also ignores calibration, slope, intercept, and sign-specific error.
Only one arbitrary displacement magnitude, one model, one checkpoint, one validation sample, and aggregate final frames are examined.
No random/untrained, element-only, atom-reference, simple GNN, standard explanation method, or alternative OC20 model baseline establishes which patterns are specific to learned chemistry.
The analysis is not stratified by in-domain versus out-of-domain OC20 splits or by the model's actual energy/force error, although the conclusion identifies this as necessary future work.
Static output sensitivity does not reveal hidden representations, message-passing pathways, sufficiency, causal mediation, or whether the apparent concept is used for correct predictions.

Several appendix density plots are sharply peaked with long tails and sometimes reverse the advertised row/column ordering, so qualitative summaries can obscure element-specific counterexamples and outlier dominance.
The workshop paper does not provide a complete reproducibility package for the exact sample, checkpoint identity, preprocessing choices, or perturbation code.
failure_modes: A model can memorize atomic reference energies or embedding similarity and reproduce periodic-table trends without learning context-dependent bonding chemistry.
An off-manifold deletion or substitution can activate arbitrary extrapolation behavior that looks smooth because the neural network is smooth, not because the response is physically correct.
Species composition can explain the adsorbate/surface/subsurface ordering even when the network attends to the wrong neighbors or produces wrong DFT energies.
A separately predicted force field can correlate locally with energy differences yet have nonzero curl, path-dependent work, unstable molecular dynamics, or ill-defined geometry optimization.
Choosing the perturbation direction from the force and then discarding force signs can manufacture a positive relationship even when quantitative finite differences are badly miscalibrated.
At a truly stationary relaxed structure, force components are near zero and noise or incomplete relaxation can dominate both the direction choice and within-system correlation.
Large heterogeneous systems contribute many correlated coordinate points to one Pearson coefficient, allowing a small number of high-force atoms or outliers to determine the result.
Mean energy changes for a rare element or replacement can be based on very different system counts, making density comparisons visually persuasive but statistically unstable.
A globally plausible aggregate can hide catalyst-specific failures, adversarial substitutions, or OOD splits where explanations invert.
The same perturbation map can arise from multiple internal mechanisms, so treating it as a unique explanation can lead model debugging toward the wrong component.
reusable_insights: Separate three questions in scientific-model interpretation: is a response intuitively structured, is it numerically correct against a physical oracle, and is the explanation faithful to the model's internal causal computation?
For atomistic counterfactuals, prefer chemically valid transformations or re-relaxed structures and pair every model response with DFT labels on a carefully selected, tractable subset.
Normalize composition-changing energy interventions with explicit elemental reference conventions and matched controls before interpreting raw total-energy differences as atom importance.
Test chemical similarity with continuous, preregistered property distances and matched substitution sets instead of relying only on periodic-table grid hops.

For direct force heads, compare F_k with negative two-sided finite differences across multiple step sizes, then test curl, closed-loop work, long-horizon dynamics, and geometry-optimization convergence.
Include nulls such as random weights, permuted atomic embeddings, atom-reference-only predictors, simple local models, and conservative energy-gradient architectures in perturbation studies.
Use hierarchical resampling over bulk material and adsorbate identity, report effect sizes and uncertainty, and inspect both distributions and system-level counterexamples.

Stratify explanations by ground-truth prediction error, in-domain/OOD split, element frequency, local coordination, and trajectory stage to learn when intuitive behavior actually predicts reliability.
Interactive atom maps are valuable debugging interfaces when linked to provenance, DFT error, uncertainty, alternative models, and reversible filtering rather than presented as standalone validation.
A sign-selected correlation is often an algebraic sanity check; design diagnostics around residuals from the governing equation, not merely the expected sign.
open_questions: Do deletion and substitution trends remain after matching atom species, coordination number, neighborhood geometry, bulk material, and energy-reference contributions?
How often do GemNet-OC perturbation responses agree quantitatively with new DFT calculations, and does that agreement predict ordinary S2EF error or stable relaxation?
Would conservative energy-gradient models and direct-force models differ in two-sided finite-difference residuals, curl, closed-loop work, and long-horizon dynamics on OC20-like systems?
Which attribution method best recovers known causal motifs in 3D catalyst systems under synthetic ground truth and physically valid interventions?
Can internal relevance propagation or causal mediation connect an output sensitivity to specific GemNet-OC messages, angular channels, or element embeddings?
How stable are the conclusions across checkpoints, seeds, GemNet-OC variants, SCN, EquiformerV2, later foundation potentials, and OC20 ID/OOD splits?
What adaptive DFT sampling strategy can validate the most informative perturbations without evaluating the entire combinatorial perturbation set?
Can counterexamples in the appendix reveal data imbalance, periodic embedding shortcuts, missing long-range physics, or systematic catalyst-family failures?

What human-facing interactive design best presents perturbation magnitude, model uncertainty, DFT discrepancy, local environment, and competing explanations without implying unwarranted causal certainty?

competitive_landscape.title: GNNExplainer: Generating Explanations for Graph Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: foundational perturbation-based graph explanation method cited by the paper
competitive_landscape.difference: GNNExplainer optimizes a compact subgraph and feature mask tied to a prediction through mutual information, whereas this paper uses hand-designed one-atom interventions and raw output changes. The simpler OC20 workflow is accessible and domain-specific, but provides no learned sparse explanation, fidelity metric, stability assessment, or ground-truth explanation benchmark.

competitive_landscape.title: Quantitative Evaluation of Explainable Graph Neural Networks for Molecular Property Prediction
competitive_landscape.difference: Rao et al. construct three levels of quantitative ground truth and compare several attribution methods, finding method/model interactions and strong GradInput/Integrated Gradients results. This paper instead analyzes a harder 3D catalyst force field at OC20 scale, but validates explanations only by qualitative chemical intuition and has no competing explainer baseline.

competitive_landscape.title: Analyzing Atomic Interactions in Molecules as Learned by Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: subsequent direct competitor for interpreting learned atomistic interactions
competitive_landscape.difference: Esders et al. use higher-order relevance explanations on SchNet and PaiNN to quantify interaction strength, range, many-body character, and extensive versus intensive prediction strategies, then connect violations of physical principles to unstable molecular dynamics. It moves beyond single-input sensitivity and directly tests whether explanation-derived deviations predict simulation failure.

competitive_landscape.title: On Explaining Equivariant Graph Networks via Improved Relevance Propagation
competitive_landscape.difference: EquiGX derives layer-wise relevance rules for tensor products, equivariant nonlinearities, geometric distances, and directions, and evaluates them on synthetic motifs with ground-truth explanations plus real 3D tasks. The present paper is architecture-agnostic at the input/output boundary but cannot attribute GemNet-OC's internal equivariant computations or quantitatively score explanation fidelity.

competitive_landscape.title: The Dark Side of the Forces: Assessing Non-Conservative Force Models for Atomistic Machine Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: subsequent direct audit of the paper's energy-force consistency claim
competitive_landscape.difference: Bigi et al. show that directly predicted non-conservative forces can cause ill-defined optimization and unstable dynamics even when ordinary force accuracy is strong, and argue that conservation is difficult to learn. That evidence makes this paper's positive local Pearson histogram an insufficient validation: finite-difference residuals, curl, path work, and downstream simulation behavior are needed.

competitive_landscape.title: EquiformerV2: Improved Equivariant Transformer for Scaling to Higher-Degree Representations
competitive_landscape.relationship: later high-performing OC20 model that changes the comparison frontier
competitive_landscape.difference: EquiformerV2 reports better OC20 force and energy accuracy than earlier state of the art while scaling higher-degree equivariant features. Because this paper studies one 2022 GemNet-OC checkpoint, its claimed chemistry patterns must be rerun across newer architectures to establish whether they diagnose correctness, reflect a general data shortcut, or are checkpoint-specific.

competitive_landscape.title: What is Your Force Field Really Learning? Gaining Scientific Intuition with A Dual-Level Explainability Framework
competitive_landscape.difference: DUAL-X combines model-centric Grad-CAM localization with SHAP over physically meaningful SOAP descriptors to distinguish where a MACE force field focuses from what geometric interactions it prioritizes under different training strategies. It offers a more explicit internal-to-physical explanation bridge, though its human-defined descriptors and feature-dependence assumptions introduce their own faithfulness limits.

novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference: this short workshop paper appears to be an early, useful application of large-scale input perturbation analysis specifically to GemNet-OC on OC20, with an unusually approachable set of rotatable catalyst visualizations and three intuitive dataset-level checks. The broad methodology was not novel—graph perturbation explainers and molecular XAI already existed—and the experiments do not support the stronger wording that the model learned reasonable chemical concepts. They show that one checkpoint has qualitatively structured sensitivities on 10,000 unlabelled counterfactuals. Subsequent work on quantitative molecular-XAI benchmarks, internal relevance propagation for equivariant GNNs, interaction-level MLFF analysis, and non-conservative-force pathologies substantially raises the standard: physically valid counterfactuals, oracle labels, causal/fidelity evaluation, multiple models, and dynamical conservation tests are now necessary.
reviewer_notes: All 12 pages were read, including references and every appendix plot. Because the recovered text has two-column and rotated-text warnings, rendered PDF pages 3-8 and 11-12 were inspected directly; the values, plotted orderings, appendix counterexamples, Figure 8 histogram, and sign of the displacement protocol were verified visually. Current direct competitors were checked in primary arXiv, PMLR, and OpenReview sources on 2026-08-23. A central technical correction is that the paper says both 'force is the gradient' and 'move toward the force,' but its explicit examples move opposite the predicted force; with the standard F = -grad E convention, this is movement up the predicted energy gradient. Consequently, the positive force-magnitude/energy-increase correlation is partly built into the perturbation design and should be replaced by signed, two-sided finite-difference and conservation residuals.
